groupings.title: Robust Data Backup (DB)
groupings.description:
Be prepared to recover gracefully from an incident. Employ a backup solution that
automatically and continuously backs up your business-critical data and system configurations. Ensure the
backed-up data is stored securely (encrypted) offsite or in the cloud and allows for at least 30 days of
rollback. Periodically test your ability to recover data from backup.

groupings.title: Web Browser Management and DNS Filtering (BM)
groupings.description: Avoid danger and filter out connections to unauthorized websites, suspicious domains names, and known malicious domains names that will make you vulnerable to malware (such as ransomware) and phishing. Leverage DNS filtering, also known as DNS Blocking or DNS Firewall, with integrated threat intelligence. A number of effective commercial solutions are available ranging from free to low cost that make this an especially recommended action.

groupings.title: Phishing Prevention and Awareness (PP)
groupings.description: Take steps to increase and maintain awareness of Phishing threats. Conduct ongoing phishing and social engineering campaigns that randomly and periodically send simulated phishing emails to personnel. Offer phishing awareness training to staff which will assist in recognizing and reporting phishing attacks. Utilize an SMTP (mail server) proxy that employs reputational (IP, URL, and sender) and traditional anti-SPAM and content filtering features.

groupings.title: Network Perimeter Monitoring (NM)
groupings.description: Look for suspicious activity and react faster. Monitor internet traffic into and out of your organization. Be sure to use a product or service with integrated threat intelligence and consider subscribing to additional indicator sharing feeds, such as the Automated Indicator Sharing service provided by DHS, to automatically identify attacks and known bad actors.

groupings.title: Asset Management (AM)
groupings.description:
Protecting your systems requires knowing which devices are connected to your network, which applications are in use, who has access to them, and the security measures in place. A cyber-ready business keeps its systems up-to-date and secure. These actions can support a proactive risk management culture and limit the risk of compromise.

Remove unsupported or unauthorized hardware and software. Supported hardware and software generally allow you to receive updates and patches for vulnerabilities that otherwise are not available for unauthorized and unsupported assets. Inventory authorized hardware and software throughout your organization. Know the physical location and user of the hardware to keep patching updates current. This also allows for any unauthorized hardware or software to be identified and removed.

groupings.title: Patch and Update Management (PM)
groupings.description: Make it generally harder for the bad guys by eliminating known vulnerabilities. Obtain, test, and deploy software and firmware patches as quickly as practical. Enable automatic updates whenever possible. Replace end of life (EOL) / unsupported operating systems, applications, and hardware with vendor supported versions/models.

groupings.title: User and Access Management (UM)
groupings.description: Implement policies, processes, and technologies that ensure only authorized users are granted the minimum privileges needed. Identify and deactivate unused accounts, eliminate shared accounts, remove unnecessary privileges, and enforce strong password policies. Monitor and analyze user activities for anomalous behavior such as access attempts outside of normal operating hours or from unusual locations. Consider mechanisms that are stronger than password authentication such as biometrics, one-time passwords and tokens for sensitive applications and functions. Multi-factor authentication, in particular, is highly recommended starting with privileged users first, then expanding to all users. User and Access Management will be a daunting and complex activity—and there is no "one size fits all" solution. Adopt a strategy appropriate to your organization and leverage a staged approach.

groupings.title: Application Integrity and Allowlist (AI)
groupings.description: Ensure your applications perform in a secure and as-intended manner by instituting an Application Integrity policy that allows only approved, authorized software and their libraries to load and execute. Monitor the integrity of approved applications with periodic checks of file hashes to ensure no unauthorized modifications have been made. As with identity and access management—due to the complexity and effort required—consider a staged, gradually phased-in approach starting with high impact endpoints (e.g. domain controllers, application servers, databases), followed by any remaining support systems, and ending with any remaining user workstations or endpoints.

groupings.title: Incident Response (IR)
groupings.description:
Lead development of an incident response and disaster recovery plan outlining roles and responsibilities. Test it often. Incident response plans and disaster recovery plans are crucial to information security, but they are separate plans. Incident response mainly focuses on information asset protection, while disaster recovery plans focus on business continuity. Once you develop a plan, test the plan using realistic simulations (known as "war-gaming"), where roles and responsibilities are assigned to the people who manage cyber incident responses. This ensures that your plan is effective and that you have the appropriate people involved in the plan. Disaster recovery plans minimize recovery time by efficiently recovering critical systems.

Plan, prepare, and conduct drills for cyber-attacks and incidents as you would a fire or robbery. Make your reaction to cyber incidents or system outages an extension of your other business contingency plans. This involves having incident response plans and procedures, trained staff, assigned roles and responsibilities, and incident communications plans.

groupings.title: Risk Management (RM)
groupings.description: Lead investment in cybersecurity by investing in capabilities for your organization and staff. This includes not only investments in technological capabilities, but also a continuous investment in cybersecurity training and awareness capabilities for your organization’s personnel. Have conversations with your staff, business partners, vendors, managed service providers, and others within your supply chain. Use risk assessments to identify and prioritize allocation of resources and cyber investment.

questions.title: BM:B.Q01
questions.text: Is malicious web content being blocked using DNS filtering via methods like DNS resolvers and DNS firewalls?
questions.supplemental:
Question Intent: To determine if DNS filtering is being employed to block malicious web content.

Domain Name System (DNS) protection blocks dangerous sites and filters out unwanted content. A DNS look-up service works by translating a URL – a news site for example – to the actual IP address of that destination. Much like a phonebook that ties a person’s name to their phone number. DNS servers ensure devices are connecting through a secure portal. This adds a layer of protection against malware, phishing, and other viruses.

Possible actions:
  • Leverage DNS filtering, also known as DNS Blocking, DNS Firewall, or protective DNS, with integrated threat intelligence. DNS filtering is a method used to filter out undesirable and malicious content. A number of effective commercial solutions are available ranging from free to low cost.
  • Filter out connections to unauthorized websites, suspicious domain names, and known malicious domain names associated with malware and phishing.
Criteria for “Yes” Response:
  • DNS filtering is actively employed by the organization to block malicious web content.

questions.title: DB:B.Q01
questions.text: Are important systems and data backed up daily to an offsite location with the ability to restore multiple versions back at least 30 days?
questions.supplemental:
Question Intent: To determine if important systems are backed up daily to an offsite location with the ability to restore back at least 30 days.

Learn to protect your information as it is stored, processed, or transmitted. Identify information critical to operations stored on your network. Have plans in place to help recover and restore systems, networks, and data from known good backups. Regular backups protect against ransomware and other forms of malware attacks. Use on-site and remote backup methods to protect vulnerable information. Periodic testing of the organization’s backup and storage procedures ensures continued validity as operational conditions change.

Online and cloud storage backup services can help protect against data loss and provide encryption as an added level of security. Identify key files you need access to if online backups are unavailable when you do not have an internet connection.

Possible actions:
  • Employ a backup solution that automatically and continuously backs up your business-critical data and system configurations.
  • Leverage protections for backups, including physical security, encryption, and offline copies.
  • To increase the chances of recovering lost or corrupted data, follow the 3-2-1 rule:
    • 3 – Keep three copies of any important file: one primary and two backups.
    • 2 – Keep the files on two different media types to protect against different types of hazards.
    • 1 – Store one copy – or “go bag” – off-site (e.g., outside the home or business facility).
Criteria for “Yes” Response:
  • Important systems and data are backed up daily.
  • And, backed up to an offsite location.
  • And, created with the ability to restore multiple versions back at least 30 days.

questions.title: PP:B.Q01
questions.text: Are annual tabletop exercises that include phishing response scenarios conducted?
questions.supplemental:
Question Intent: To determine if the organization conducts tabletop exercises that include phishing response scenarios at least annually.

Plan, prepare, and conduct drills for cyber-attacks, like phishing, and incidents as you would a fire or robbery. This involves having incident response plans and procedures, trained staff, assigned roles and responsibilities, and incident communications plans.

A tabletop exercise is a discussion-based walk through of the incident response plan based on a simulated emergency described in a particular threat scenario. Team members will discuss their roles and response to a particular situation or incident that is described in the scenario. This helps the organization identify flaws or gaps in the organization's response and helps train and better prepare team members to respond in a real situation.

Possible actions:
  • Ensure that incident response plans account for cyber-attacks, like phishing and ransomware.
  • Conduct drills such as tabletop exercises and ensure those exercises include phishing response scenarios.
Criteria for “Yes” Response:
  • Tabletop exercises that test the organizations incident response plan and include phishing response scenarios are conducted at least annually.

questions.title: NM:B.Q01
questions.text: Is perimeter network traffic monitored?
questions.supplemental:
Question Intent: To determine if perimeter network traffic is being actively monitored by the organization.

Manage perimeter network components and monitor internet traffic into and out of your organization. Establish a monitoring strategy to identify unusual activity that could indicate an attack. A continuous monitoring capability should allow staff to be alerted and respond to security incidents more quickly.

Possible actions:
  • Deploy intrusion detection or intrusion prevention systems. Intrusion detection and intrusion prevention systems are examples of a technologies capable of scanning and analyzing internet traffic for malicious activity, reporting on that activity, and potentially taking action against it.
  • Deploy network traffic analyzers. Network traffic analyzers can monitor both the internet traffic that crosses the network perimeter and all of the internal network communications by analyzing network traffic and flow records.
Criteria for “Yes” Response:
  • All perimeter network traffic is actively being monitored to identify malicious activity.

questions.title: PM:B.Q01
questions.text: Is all public-facing software patched for vulnerabilities within 15 days for vulnerabilities rated as “Critical” and 30 days for vulnerabilities rated as “High”?
questions.supplemental:
Question Intent: To determine if all public facing systems are patched within the prescribed timeframe based on guidance and rating (15 days for “Critical” and 30 days for “High”)

What are patches? Patches are software and operating system (OS) updates that address security vulnerabilities within a program or product. Software vendors may choose to release updates to fix performance bugs, as well as to provide enhanced security features.

When possible, leverage automatic updates for all operating systems and third-party software. An easy step is to establish and maintain network security/patching procedures to prevent attacks by configuring functions and programs necessary for security. Be sure to obtain, test, and deploy the latest versions of operating systems and applications.

Enabling automatic updates should be done with care. Take the time to determine and establish an appropriately architected patching infrastructure and process, and ensure it meets the business need. For example, a centralized solution may be best as you do not want every system on the network obtaining patches individually from the internet.

Operational environments may present unique requirements. The security challenges facing Industrial Control Systems (ICS) will require additional attention and consideration. It may not be possible to employ automated patching methods to all ICS environment assets. It is very important that vendor patches be tested in a test environment that closely mimics the production environment prior to deploying the patch to the production environment.

A possible software patching process:

1. Plan
  • Use the organization's inventory of hardware and software assets to help determine which patches need to be applied and to help ensure that all applications and devices are kept patched.
  • Consider using the inventory of assets to group assets by the level of risk and impact they would pose to the organization if they were disrupted.
  • Consider using the inventory to streamline and consolidate the number of software versions in the environment. This will reduce the complexity and overhead of the patching process.
  • Establish sources of vendor patching information and track vendor security update announcements.
2. Analyze and Test
  • Analyze the effects of the patch in your environment and determine if you will encounter exceptions where a patch can’t be deployed immediately. Until the patch can be applied, consider the types of compensating controls you can put in place to protect those assets.
  • Establish a test environment and if possible, test the patch before it is deployed to the entire environment. Expect bumps in the road.
  • Develop a plan for rolling out the patch. If the testing was successful, you may consider planning to roll out the patch in a phased approach. Patch a small set of production systems to evaluate the effects before rolling it out to the rest of the environment. You may also consider multiple phases in your approach.
  • A backout plan should also be developed in case there are issues.
3. Implement
  • Use the organization’s change control process to get approval to implement the patch. Much of the information collected above will need to be part of the change request.
  • Consider backing up the appropriate assets prior to pushing out the patch.
  • Once the change is approved, patch the appropriate assets according to the plan.
  • Closely monitor critical assets for issues and implement the backout plan if necessary.
4. Review
  • Go back and review all the systems that were patched and verify that the patch was applied. It is not unusual to find that the patch was unsuccessful on a small percentage of systems
  • Reapply the patch to the systems that the patch was unsuccessful for.
  • Use any lessons learned to improve the patch process.
Possible considerations:
  • Enable automatic software updates whenever possible. This will ensure that software updates are installed as quickly as possible.
  • When possible, do not use unsupported end of life (EOL) software.
  • Always visit vendor sites directly rather than clicking on advertisements or email links.
  • Avoid software updates while using untrusted networks.
  • New vulnerabilities are continually emerging, but the best defense against attackers exploiting patched vulnerabilities is simple: keep your software up to date. This is one of the most effective measures you can take to protect your computer, phone, and other digital devices.
Vulnerabilities are based on the Common Vulnerabilities and Exposures (CVE) vulnerability naming standard and are organized according to severity, determined by the Common Vulnerability Scoring System (CVSS) standard. The division of high, medium, and low severities correspond to the following scores:
  1. High: vulnerabilities with a CVSS base score of 7.0–10.0
  2. Medium: vulnerabilities with a CVSS base score of 4.0–6.9
  3. Low: vulnerabilities with a CVSS base score of 0.0–3.9
Criteria for “Yes” Response:
  • All public facing software with vulnerabilities rated “High” are patched within 30 days.
  • And, all public facing software with vulnerabilities rated as “Critical” are patched within 15 days.

questions.title: UM:B.Q01
questions.text: Are strong and unique passwords implemented throughout the entire organization?
questions.supplemental:
Question Intent: To determine if all accounts require strong and unique passwords.

Passwords are the most common means of authentication, but only work if they are complex and confidential. Many cyber-attacks occur due to weak and easy-to-guess passwords, so all passwords should be strong and unique, such as a sentence with numeric and non-numeric digits. Although intentionally misspelling a word ("daytt" instead of "date") may offer some protection against specific types of attacks (e.g. dictionary attacks) an even better method is to rely on a series of words and use memory techniques, or mnemonics, to help you remember how to decode it. Some hackers are more sophisticated and use algorithms to figure out passwords, so consider mechanisms that are stronger than password authentication such as biometrics, one-time passwords, and tokens for sensitive applications and functions.

The National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST) has developed specific guidelines for strong passwords. According to NIST guidance, you should consider using the longest password or passphrase permissible (8–64 characters) when you can. For example, "Pattern2baseball#4mYmiemale!" would be a strong password because it has 28 characters and includes the upper and lowercase letters, numbers, and special characters.

Possible actions:

  • Use multi-factor authentication when available.
  • Use different passwords on different systems and accounts.
  • Don't use passwords that are based on personal information that can be easily accessed or guessed.
  • Use the longest password or passphrase permissible by each password system.
  • Don't use words that can be found in any dictionary of any language.
  • Develop mnemonics to remember complex passwords.
  • Consider using a password manager program to protect and keep track of your passwords.

Criteria for “Yes” Response:
  • All accounts are required to use strong and unique passwords to access all systems

questions.title: AI:B.Q01
questions.text: Is there a list of known bad software (a “Blocklist”), and is the software on that list being blocked?
questions.supplemental:
Question Intent: To determine if there is a documented list of known bad or malicious software (a “blocklist”) and is the blocklist used to prevent known software from executing on the organization’s systems.

A blocklist is a list of discrete entities, such as IP addresses, email addresses, URLs, runtime processes, or applications that have been previously determined to be associated with malicious activity. An application blocklist is a list of applications and application components (libraries, configuration files, etc.) that are used to block known bad applications/software and permit all other. Antivirus software is a good example of a technology that blocks known bad activity. Blocklist enforcement typically blocks execution of items on the blocklist but allows everything else to be executed.

Criteria for “Yes” Response:
  • The organization has documented a list of known bad software (a “blocklist”);
  • And, the organization has implemented this list and is actively stopping the software on the blocklist from executing.

questions.title: RM:I.Q01
questions.text: Does the organization perform business impact assessments?
questions.supplemental:
Question Intent: To determine if the organization performs business impact assessments as part of its service continuity program.
The Business Impact Analysis (BIA) is a foundational element of a service continuity program. The BIA measures the effects of a disruption on an organization’s services and how they impact changes over time.

Leverage business impact assessments to prioritize resources and identify which systems must be recovered first. Business impact analysis helps identify and prioritize critical systems, information, and assets. This information determines contingency requirements and priorities for critical information and services. It also allows planning for disruption impacts and identifies allowable outage times. This enables personnel to develop and prioritize recovery strategies that can be used.
Possible Actions:
  • Define business impact analysis characteristics.
    • The BIA considers the impact of disruptions over time and provides requirements for the development of continuity plans. Consider the best time frames for capturing impact, for example, four hours, one day, two days, or even days, weeks, or months.
    • The BIA is the key process tool used to establish continuity requirements and prioritize business services’ importance to meeting an organization’s mission. Consider the requirements that should be collected—for example, resources required and their relative importance.
    • The BIA identifies what to recover and when that recovery needs to be completed. Consider which services must be up and running and when.
  • Establish a link to risk assessments. Risk assessments help identify the key exposures to consider in the BIA by providing insights into the likelihood and potential impact of various disruption threats, whether natural or man-made. Leverage existing risk assessments that the organization may have conducted to
    • obtain input to the BIA and integrate with evaluation and mitigation activities already underway. Typically, groups involved in operational risk, enterprise risk, finance, audits, or compliance are good sources of information on previous risk assessments.
    • identify the essential services of the organization. Previous risk assessment documentation or senior leaders can be consulted when establishing this list.
    • determine the priority of services that are most essential or that need to get back online fastest in the event of a disruption. Service owners, managers, and senior leadership are good sources for establishing priorities.
  • Determine how to measure the impact of a service disruption. Impact information is usually measured in dollars, customers affected, reputational impact, and regulatory noncompliance. These measures of impact can inform the development of continuity requirements and strategies. In many instances, organizations look to the BIA information to develop a business case for investment in mitigation activities. This strategy aspect of continuity planning is a core driver of continuity process management. Organizations doing continuity planning must weigh spending and investment against risk. The continuity strategy decision process can clarify the risk tolerance of the organization, for example, a willingness to accept the risk of longer recovery times to keep costs down. See CRR Resource Guide Service Continuity Management v1.1, Appendix A, Business Impact Analysis Template.
Criteria for “Yes” Response:
  • The organization performs business impact assessments to identify critical business services and assets.

questions.title: IR:B.Q01
questions.text: Has the organization developed an incident response plan?
questions.supplemental:
Question Intent: To determine if the organization has a documented plan for responding to incidents.

Determine how much of your organization’s operations are dependent on IT. Consider how much your organization relies on information technology to conduct business and make it a part of your culture to plan for contingencies in the event of a cyber incident. Identify and prioritize your organization’s critical assets and the associated impacts to operations if an incident were to occur. Ask the questions that are necessary to understanding your security planning, operations, and security-related goals. Develop an understanding of how long it would take to restore normal operations. Resist the “it can’t happen here” pattern of thinking. Instead, focus cyber risk discussions on “what-if” scenarios and develop an incident response plan to prepare for various cyber events and scenarios.

Lead development of an incident response plan outlining roles and responsibilities. Test it often. Incident response plans and disaster recovery plans are crucial to information security, but they are separate plans. Incident response mainly focuses on information asset protection, while disaster recovery plans focus on business continuity.

Having a defined process for identifying, analyzing, responding to, and learning from incidents that interrupt an organization’s operations provides consistent response to cybersecurity incidents and ensures that objectives are met when handling an incident. Without a defined process, an organization’s incident response might omit actions that the organization considers important. An incident management plan describes how the organization will respond to cybersecurity incidents. The objective of the plan should be translated into specific actions assigned to individuals or groups to perform when an incident occurs.

The incident response plan should address, at a minimum:

  • the organization’s approach to incident management
  • the structure of the incident management process
  • the requirements and objectives of the incident management process
  • a description of how the organization will identify events, triage and analyze incidents, respond and recover from incidents, and improve its response capabilities over time
  • the roles and responsibilities (including establishing key stakeholders) necessary to carry out the plan
  • applicable training needs and requirements
  • resources that will be required to meet plan objectives
  • relevant costs and budgets associated with incident management activities

The following sections lay out the discrete steps for developing a plan that implements the incident management process as described above.

Possible Actions: Create an Incident Response Plan

  1. Obtain support for incident management planning.
  2. Establish an event detection process.
  3. Establish a triage and analysis process.
  4. Establish an incident declaration process.
  5. Establish an incident response and recovery process.
  6. Establish an incident communications process.
  7. Establish a post-incident analysis and improvement process.
  8. Assign roles and responsibilities for incident management, including establishing appropriate stakeholders for escalation and resolution.

Criteria for “Yes” Response:

  • The organization has a documented plan for responding to incidents.

questions.supplemental:
Question Intent: To determine if web browser security settings are being managed by the organization.

Content filtering applied to external websites can prevent attackers from delivering malicious code to desktop applications. Firewalls can also deny traffic to potentially harmful sites while allowing access to acceptable applications.
Updating the browsers security settings can make it much harder for malware to get installed. As an example, settings can be employed to reduce the ability of installing plugins and other add-ons and to disable certain types of content from automatically executing.

questions.title: PP:B.Q02
questions.text: Are users trained to recognize cyber threats like phishing?
questions.supplemental:
Question Intent: To determine if all staff are trained to recognize cyber threats like Phishing attacks.
Your staff is often the first line of defense for your organization. Investing in your personnel reduces vulnerabilities and drives a culture of ownership. They must be equipped to recognize cybersecurity risks such as phishing scams, password hacks, and outdated anti-malware, as well as trained to respond and share information appropriately. Regular training helps employees understand their role in cybersecurity, regardless of technical expertise, and the actions they take help keep your organization and customers secure.
Training your staff and promoting cyber awareness does not mean you have to create training materials from scratch. Many professional organizations, industry associations and academic institutions, as well as private sector and government sources, provide ready-to-use cybersecurity training resources at no cost.
Training should focus on threats employees encounter, like phishing emails, suspicious events to watch for, and simple best practices individual employees can adopt to reduce risk. Each aware employee strengthens your organization against attack, and act as another “sensor” to identify an attack.
Possible actions:
  • Identify available training resources through professional associations, academic institutions, private sector, and government sources.
  • Train personnel about risks like phishing and business email compromise.
  • Deliver regular updates and reminders to keep everyone aware of current threats and how to handle them if encountered.
  • Ensure employees know how and to whom to report suspicious emails, possible phishing attempts and other anomalous activity.
Criteria for “Yes” Response:
  • All personnel are trained to recognize cyber threats like phishing through awareness training and other means.

questions.text: Is internal network traffic monitored?
questions.supplemental:
Question Intent: To determine if the internal network traffic is being actively monitored by the organization.

Learn what is happening on your network. Manage internal network components, host and device components, data at rest and in transit, and user behavior and activities. Actively maintaining this information will give you a baseline for security testing and making security-based decisions. A continuous monitoring capability should increase the speed of detection and response and allow staff to be alerted and respond more quickly to security incidents.

Possible Actions:

  • Deploy network-based intrusion detection and/or intrusion prevention devices where appropriate.
  • Deploy host-based intrusion prevention solutions where appropriate.
  • Collect and evaluate network traffic flow logs.

Criteria for “Yes” Response:

questions.title: AM:B.Q02
questions.text: Has the organization removed all unsupported hardware and software from its operating environment?
questions.supplemental:
Question Intent: To determine if the organization has identified and removed all unsupported hardware and software from its operating environment.

Remove unsupported hardware and software. Supported hardware and software generally allow you to receive updates and patches for vulnerabilities that otherwise are not available for unsupported assets.

If hardware or software is unsupported, yet necessary for the fulfillment of the enterprise’s mission, document an exception detailing mitigating controls and residual risk acceptance. For any unsupported hardware or software without an exception documentation, designate as unauthorized. Review the hardware and software list to periodically verify support.

Operational environments may present unique requirements. The security challenges facing Industrial Control Systems (ICS) will require additional attention and consideration. For example, many utilize proprietary protocols and may not have the ability to support security software that is commonly used in a traditional Information Technology (IT) environment.

ICS network architectures typically differ from traditional IT environments and may require the organization to employ compensating controls. Applying security controls to ICS often rely on segmentation and boundary control between the IT and OT domains, and careful control design around local and remote connectivity to reduce attack vectors used to gain access to ICS networks.

Possible Actions:
  • Inventory authorized hardware and software throughout your organization.
  • Know the physical location and user of the hardware and software to keep patching updates current. This also allows for any unauthorized hardware or software to be identified and removed.
  • Using the inventory, determine and remove all unsupported hardware or software.
  • Other considerations for ICS:
    • Obtain a list of recommended and supported hardware and software directly from the ICS manufactures and vendors.
    • Evaluate removing unsupported hardware and software. If problematic evaluate adding compensating controls to protect the environment.
    • Track end of life and end of support notices and ensure cybersecurity requirements are considered as part of any future sourcing and procurement processes.

Criteria for “Yes” Response:
  • The organization identifies and, where appropriate, removes all unsupported hardware and software from its operating environment.

questions.title: PM:B.Q02
questions.text: Are all internal-facing software and firewalls patched for vulnerabilities within 30 days for both vulnerabilities rated as “Critical” and for vulnerabilities rated as “High”?
questions.supplemental:
Question Intent: To determine if all internal-facing systems and firewalls are patched within the prescribed timeframe based on guidance and rating (30 days for both Critical” and “High”).

What are patches? Patches are software and operating system (OS) updates that address security vulnerabilities within a program or product. Software vendors may choose to release updates to fix performance bugs, as well as to provide enhanced security features.

When possible, leverage automatic updates for all operating systems and third-party software. An easy step is to establish and maintain network security/patching procedures to prevent attacks by configuring functions and programs necessary for security. Be sure to obtain, test, and deploy the latest versions of operating systems and applications.

Enabling automatic updates should be done with care. Take the time to determine and establish an appropriately architected patching infrastructure and process, and ensure it meets the business need. For example, a centralized solution may be best as you do not want every system on the network obtaining patches individually from the internet.

Operational environments may present unique requirements. The security challenges facing Industrial Control Systems (ICS) will require additional attention and consideration. It may not be possible to employ automated patching methods to all ICS environment assets. It is very important that vendor patches be tested in a test environment that closely mimics the production environment prior to deploying the patch to the production environment.

A possible software patching process:

1. Plan
  • Use the organization's inventory of hardware and software assets to help determine which patches need to be applied and to help ensure that all applications and devices are kept patched.
  • Consider using the inventory of assets to group assets by the level of risk and impact they would pose to the organization if they were disrupted.
  • Consider using the inventory to streamline and consolidate the number of software versions in the environment. This will reduce the complexity and overhead of the patching process.
  • Establish sources of vendor patching information and track vendor security update announcements.
2. Analyze and Test
  • Analyze the effects of the patch in your environment and determine if you will encounter exceptions where a patch can’t be deployed immediately. Until the patch can be applied, consider the types of compensating controls you can put in place to protect those assets.
  • Establish a test environment and if possible, test the patch before it is deployed to the entire environment. Expect bumps in the road.
  • Develop a plan for rolling out the patch. If the testing was successful, you may consider planning to roll out the patch in a phased approach. Patch a small set of production systems to evaluate the effects before rolling it out to the rest of the environment. You may also consider multiple phases in your approach.
  • A backout plan should also be developed in case there are issues.
3. Implement
  • Use the organization’s change control process to get approval to implement the patch. Much of the information collected above will need to be part of the change request.
  • Consider backing up the appropriate assets prior to pushing out the patch.
  • Once the change is approved, patch the appropriate assets according to the plan.
  • Closely monitor critical assets for issues and implement the backout plan if necessary.
4. Review
  • Go back and review all the systems that were patched and verify that the patch was applied. It is not unusual to find that the patch was unsuccessful on a small percentage of systems.
  • Reapply the patch to the systems that the patch was unsuccessful for.
  • Use any lessons learned to improve the patch process.
Possible considerations:

  • Enable automatic software updates whenever possible. This will ensure that software updates are installed as quickly as possible.
  • When possible, do not use unsupported end of life (EOL) software.
  • Always visit vendor sites directly rather than clicking on advertisements or email links.
  • Avoid software updates while using untrusted networks.
  • New vulnerabilities are continually emerging, but the best defense against attackers exploiting patched vulnerabilities is simple: keep your software up to date. This is one of the most effective measure you can take to protect your computer, phone, and other digital devices.
Vulnerabilities are based on the Common Vulnerabilities and Exposures (CVE) vulnerability naming standard and are organized according to severity, determined by the Common Vulnerability Scoring System (CVSS) standard. The division of high, medium, and low severities correspond to the following scores:
  1. High: vulnerabilities with a CVSS base score of 7.0–10.0
  2. Medium: vulnerabilities with a CVSS base score of 4.0–6.9
  3. Low: vulnerabilities with a CVSS base score of 0.0–3.9
Criteria for “Yes” Response:
  • All internal-facing software with vulnerabilities rated “High” or “Critical” are patched within 30 days.

questions.title: UM:I.Q02
questions.text: Is two-factor authentication implemented for all privileged (e.g. system administrators) and remote users?
questions.supplemental:
Question Intent: To determine if all privileged users (e.g. system administrators) and all remote users are required to use two-factor authentication for all system access.

Multi-factor authentication (MFA), sometimes referred to as two-factor authentication or 2FA, is a security enhancement that allows you to present two pieces of evidence – your credentials – when logging in to an account. Your credentials fall into any of these three categories: something you know (like a password or PIN), something you have (like a smart card), or something you are (like your fingerprint). Your credentials must come from two different categories to enhance security – so entering two different passwords would not be considered multi-factor.

MFA is quite simple, and organizations are focusing more than ever on creating a smooth user experience. In fact, you probably already use it in some form. For example, you’ve used MFA if you’ve:

  • swiped your bank card at the ATM and then entered your PIN (personal ID number)
  • logged into a website that sent a numeric code to your phone, which you then entered to gain access to your account.

Criteria for “Yes” Response:

  • All Privileged and remote users are required to use two-factor authentication for all system access.

questions.text: Has the organization documented a list of known approved software (an “Allowlist”)?

Question Intent: To determine if there is a documented list of known good or approved software (an “allowlist”)

An application allowlist is a list of applications and application components (libraries, configuration files, etc.) that are authorized to be present or active on a host. Application allowlists, in conjunction with application allowlisting technologies, are used to stop the execution of malware and other unauthorized software. Application allowlist technologies are designed to permit only known good activity and block all other.

Application allowlisting can be more effective at stopping unknown malware threats than conventional antivirus software and other traditional antimalware security controls. Allowlisting can be implemented using a combination of commercial tools, policies, or application execution tools. Features that implement allowlists are included in many modern endpoint security suites and other technologies.

Criteria for “Yes” Response:
  • The organization has documented an allowlist, a list of know good and approved software.

questions.text: Has the organization defined organizational risk criteria and tolerances?
questions.supplemental:
Question Intent: To determine if the organization has defined risk criteria and if risk tolerances thresholds have been defined for each criteria.
Organizational risk assessments are used, in part, to inform the security and privacy control selection process. The selection process results in an agreed-upon set of security and privacy controls addressing specific mission or business needs consistent with organizational risk tolerance.
Risk framing is most effective when conducted at the organization level and in consultation with stakeholders throughout the organization including mission, business, and system owners. The assumptions, constraints, risk tolerance, priorities, and trade-offs identified as part of the risk framing process inform the risk management strategy, which in turn informs the conduct of risk assessment, risk response, and risk monitoring activities.
Risk tolerance is defined as the level of risk or the degree of uncertainty that is acceptable to an organization.
Risk parameters may differ for each impact area. Risk tolerance parameters describe the risk measurement criteria for each impact area. Risk measurement criteria include how impact is measured, how frequently it is measured, and what is to be measured.
Risk tolerance thresholds, which trigger action, should be defined for each category of risk.
  • Risk tolerance parameters describe the risk measurement criteria for each impact area.
  • Risk tolerance thresholds are used by management to determine when a risk is in control or when it has exceeded acceptable limits.
  • Risk tolerance thresholds should be set for each category/parameter of risk that the organization establishes as a means for measuring and managing risk. For example:
    • A risk tolerance threshold for a category of risk may be whenever more than 200 users are impacted.
    • The risk tolerance threshold indicates when action needs to be taken to prevent operational disruption.
Criteria for “Yes” Response:
  • The organization has defined risk criteria and risk tolerance thresholds for each criteria of risk.

Example communications duties include the following:
  • Coordinate all media communications.
  • Review and approve all statements regarding the incident.
  • Develop both internal and external communications.
  • Coordinate recovery-related advertising with external vendors.

  • Identify stakeholders for each category of incident. Stakeholders should be predefined and include:
    • staff required to assist in incident analysis, triage, and response
    • staff potentially impacted by the incident
    • staff responsible for coordination and status communication.
  • Establish a format for incident reporting. See References for an example Incident Reporting Template.
  • Communicate/escalate incident status and response to affected parties and predefined stakeholders.

  • The organization reports and escalates all cybersecurity incidents to the proper stakeholders.

Question Intent: To determine if the organization test its data backups at least annually.

Creating and restoring backup files can help mitigate the destructive effects of a ransomware attack. Periodically test your ability to recover data from backups to verify the integrity of the backups and their ability to be restored. The more critical or important the data, the more often you should test. Test your backup strategy before you need to use it to make sure you have full read-back verification, a method of preventing errors when information is relayed or repeated in a different form to confirm its accuracy.

questions.text: Is email filtered to protect against malicious content?
questions.supplemental:
Question Intent: To determine if all email is filtered to protect against malicious content.

Web browsers and email clients are very common points of entry for attackers. Emails can be crafted to spoof users into disclosing sensitive information. Using email filtering and malware scanning at the email gateway reduces the number of malicious emails reaching the organizations staff. Outbound email can also be filtered to prevent staff from inadvertently sending malicious email and to alert the organization that there may be an issue internally.

Possible Actions:
  • Leverage email and web browser security settings to protect against spoofed or modified emails and unsecured webpages.
  • Employ spam protection mechanisms to detect and act on unsolicited messages. Spam can be transported by different means, including email, email attachments, and web accesses.
  • Customize your email settings to allow safe mail. Set the content filters to send mail containing certain words and email addresses to the spam folder and to block malicious attachments.
Criteria for “Yes” Response:
  • All email received by the organization is filtered to block malicious content.

questions.title: NM:I.Q03
questions.text: Are networks segmented to protect mission critical assets?
questions.supplemental:
Question Intent: To determine if networks are segmented to protect the organization's mission critical assets.

Segmentation divides a computer network into smaller parts. Segmenting a network will improve network performance and security by reducing the attack surface and limiting how far an attack can spread. Network traffic can then be controlled between the various parts of the network. A segmentation policy can be implemented to limit the flow of network traffic by type, source address, and destination address to name a few.

Some technologies that can be used to implement a segmentation policy include:
  • firewalls
  • access control list
  • virtual local area networks (VLANs)

questions.text: Are all software and firewalls patched for vulnerabilities within 15 days for vulnerabilities rated as “Critical” and 30 days for vulnerabilities rated as “High”?
questions.supplemental:
Question Intent: To determine if all software and firewalls are patched within the prescribed timeframe based on guidance and rating (15 days for “Critical” and 30 days for “High”).

What are patches? Patches are software and operating system (OS) updates that address security vulnerabilities within a program or product. Software vendors may choose to release updates to fix performance bugs, as well as to provide enhanced security features.

Make it generally harder for the bad guys by eliminating known vulnerabilities. Obtain, test, and deploy software and firmware patches as quickly as practical. Enable automatic updates whenever possible. Replace end of life/unsupported operating systems, applications and hardware with vendor supported versions/models.
Enabling automatic updates should be done with care. Take the time to determine and establish an appropriately architected patching infrastructure and process, and ensure it meets the business need. For example, a centralized solution may be best as you do not want every system on the network obtaining patches individually from the internet.

Operational environments may present unique requirements. The security challenges facing Industrial Control Systems (ICS) will require additional attention and consideration. It may not be possible to employ automated patching methods to all ICS environment assets. It is very important that vendor patches be tested in a test environment that closely mimics the production environment prior to deploying the patch to the production environment.

A possible software patching process:

1. Plan
  • Use the organization's inventory of hardware and software assets to help determine which patches need to be applied and to help ensure that all applications and devices are kept patched.
  • Consider using the inventory of assets to group assets by the level of risk and impact they would pose to the organization if they were disrupted.
  • Consider using the inventory to streamline and consolidate the number of software versions in the environment. This will reduce the complexity and overhead of the patching process.
  • Establish sources of vendor patching information and track vendor security update announcements.
2. Analyze and Test
  • Analyze the effects of the patch in your environment and determine if you will encounter exceptions where a patch can’t be deployed immediately. Until the patch can be applied, consider the types of compensating controls you can put in place to protect those assets.
  • Establish a test environment and if possible, test the patch before it is deployed to the entire environment. Expect bumps in the road.
  • Develop a plan for rolling out the patch. If the testing was successful, you may consider planning to roll out the patch in a phased approach. Patch a small set of production systems to evaluate the effects before rolling it out to the rest of the environment. You may also consider multiple phases in your approach.
  • A backout plan should also be developed in case there are issues.
3. Implement
  • Use the organization’s change control process to get approval to implement the patch. Much of the information collected above will need to be part of the change request.
  • Consider backing up the appropriate assets prior to pushing out the patch.
  • Once the change is approved, patch the appropriate assets according to the plan.
  • Closely monitor critical assets for issues and implement the backout plan if necessary.
4. Review
  • Go back and review all the systems that were patched and verify that the patch was applied. It is not unusual to find that the patch was unsuccessful on a small percentage of systems
  • Reapply the patch to the systems that the patch was unsuccessful for.
  • Use any lessons learned to improve the patch process.
Possible considerations:

  • Enable automatic software updates whenever possible. This will ensure that software updates are installed as quickly as possible.
  • When possible, do not use unsupported end of life (EOL) software.
  • Always visit vendor sites directly rather than clicking on advertisements or email links.
  • Avoid software updates while using untrusted networks.
  • New vulnerabilities are continually emerging, but the best defense against attackers exploiting patched vulnerabilities is simple: keep your software up to date. This is one of the most effective measure you can take to protect your computer, phone, and other digital devices.
Vulnerabilities are based on the Common Vulnerabilities and Exposures (CVE) vulnerability naming standard and are organized according to severity, determined by the Common Vulnerability Scoring System (CVSS) standard.   • Medium: vulnerabilities with a CVSS base score of 4.0–6.9
  • Low: vulnerabilities with a CVSS base score of 0.0–3.9

questions.text: Is two-factor authentication implemented for all users?
questions.supplemental:
Question Intent: To determine if all users are required to use two-factor authentication for all system access.

Multi-factor authentication (MFA), sometimes referred to as two-factor authentication or 2FA, is a security enhancement that allows you to present two pieces of evidence – your credentials – when logging in to an account. Your credentials fall into any of these three categories: something you know (like a password or PIN), something you have (like a smart card), or something you are (like your fingerprint). Your credentials must come from two different categories to enhance security – so entering two different passwords would not be considered multi-factor.

MFA is quite simple, and organizations are focusing more than ever on creating a smooth user experience. In fact, you probably already use it in some form. For example, you’ve used MFA if you’ve:
  • swiped your bank card at the ATM and then entered your PIN (personal ID number).
  • logged into a website that sent a numeric code to your phone, which you then entered to gain access to your account.

Criteria for “Yes” Response:
  • All users are required to use two-factor authentication for all systems access.

questions.supplemental:
Question Intent: To determine whether the organization considers risk inheritance and exposure between its various interconnected systems.

Organizations should consider the risk related to new or increased threats that may be introduced when systems exchange information with other systems that may have different security and privacy requirements and controls. This includes systems within the same organization and systems that are external to the organization.

Risk assessments can support a wide variety of risk-based decisions and activities including the definition of interconnection security requirements for information exchange.   • System information exchanges include connections via leased lines
  • virtual private networks
  • connections to internet service providers
  • connections and exchanges with cloud services
  • exchanges via web-based services
  • exchanges of files via file transfer protocol
  • other organization-to-organization communications.
Possible Actions:
  • Identify transitive (downstream) information exchanges with other systems
  • Verify that individuals or systems transferring data between interconnecting systems have the requisite authorizations (i.e., write permissions or privileges) prior to accepting such data.

    • interconnection security agreements
    • information exchange security agreements
    • memoranda of understanding or agreement
    • service level agreements

questions.title: UM:B.Q04
questions.text: Is the principle of least privilege enforced through policies and procedures?
questions.supplemental:
Question Intent: To determine if the principle of least privilege is enforced through policies and procedure to control user access.

Least privilege is the restriction of privileges to only those accounts that require them to perform their duties, while limiting accounts to only those privileges that are truly necessary. Doing this reduces the exposure of those privileges to a smaller, more easily manageable set of accounts. Local administrative accounts and accounts for software program management and installation are particularly powerful, but have small scopes of control and should be restricted as much as possible.

Grant access and admin permissions based on the principles of need-to-know and least privilege. Restrict user access to only the information, networks, hardware and applications necessary.

Questions to consider:
  • Are you asking why someone, or something, needs privileged access?
  • Does the marketing team need access to the company’s financial transactions?
  • Does the reservations team need access to social media sites?
  • Does a junior analyst need management-level admin / configuration privileges?
Answering these questions helps you identify and implement need-to-know and least privilege to lower the risks of malware infections, data breaches, and insider threats.

Criteria for “Yes” Response:
  • The organization enforces the principle of least privilege through policies and procedure for all user access.

questions.title: RM:A.Q04
questions.text: Does the organization apply quantitative risk analysis to remediation activities?
questions.supplemental:
Question Intent: To determine if the organization applies meaningful and measurable quantitative risk analysis to its remediation activities, which when acted upon, directly reduces the risk to the organization.
To effectively analyze metrics related to remediation activities, the organization should assess the risk management plan against its objectives using quantitative risk analysis. When risks appear to be exceeding the organization’s tolerances, action needs to be taken. Determining when risks should be addressed is often complex and hard to measure. Organizations may find that the best approach is to use a combination of metrics that are collaboratively reviewed to arrive at actionable decisions.

In applying quantitative measurements to risk analysis, it can be useful to first understand the difference between quantitative and qualitative approaches:

Qualitative measurements: typically aimed at collecting and interpreting empirical data that cannot be expressed in numbers (e.g., internal or external audit ratings on overall results: good, fair, poor).
Quantitative measurements: more formalized measures that consider both impact and probabilities:

Quantitative measure examples:
  • technical measures (e.g., availability, virus infection rates, problem reports, access violations)
  • incident and service continuity plan tested as scheduled
  • risk policy/standards exception and violation rates
  • realized risk impacts in dollars, customers, reputation, stock price, etc.
Useful / Less Useful Metrics
To illustrate the difference between a meaningful and measurable cybersecurity risk metric and one that is less useful, consider the following:
  • Useful metric: the time it takes an organization to patch a critical vulnerability across the enterprise. In this example, reducing the days it takes to patch a vulnerability directly reduces the risk to the organization.
  • Less useful metric: the number of alerts a Security Operations Center (SOC) receives in a week. There are too many variables in the number of alerts an SOC receives for this number to be consistently relevant.
Possible Actions:
  • Develop a clear understanding of the most important risks the organization is facing by prioritizing the risks. Prioritize based on impact to the organization if the risk is realized.
  • Develop reporting and quantitative risk metrics designed to measure the effectiveness of the remediation activities.
  • Establish a schedule and format for reporting on these risks.
  • Periodically report on these risks and related metrics to stakeholders, including leaders and operational managers.
  • Gather feedback from the reporting activity to improve the risk metrics and the reporting activity.
Criteria for “Yes” Response:
  • The organization applies quantitative risk analysis to its remediation activities.

questions.text: Does the organization conduct annual incident response tabletop exercises that include ransomware response scenarios?
questions.supplemental:
Question Intent: To determine if the organization conducts incident response tabletop exercises that include ransomware response scenarios at least annually.

Incident response testing includes, for example, the use of checklists, walk-through or tabletop exercises, simulations (parallel/full interrupt), and comprehensive exercises.

Organizations should conduct incident response tabletop exercises to determine the overall effectiveness of their response capabilities and to identify potential weaknesses or deficiencies. Ransomware response scenarios should be included in the testing drills.

Incident response testing can also include a determination of the effects of an incident on organizational operations (e.g., reduction in business capabilities), organizational assets, and individuals due to incident response.

Once the organization has developed its plan, the plan should be tested using realistic simulations (known as “war-gaming”), where roles and responsibilities are assigned to the people who manage cyber incident responses. This ensures the plan is effective and the appropriate people involved in the plan.

Possible Actions:

There are many approaches to testing, and the testing process may be progressive.

  • Organizations typically begin with plan reviews, proceed to tabletop walkthroughs, and finally conduct partial to full plan tests.
  • Contact lists can be exercised from the beginning, and such exercises should include alternate contacts and sometimes occur unannounced and during off hours.
  • If the organization has a process for testing service continuity plans, the testing criteria and schedule may be modified to accommodate the incident management plan.

If no testing process exists, create a process, including testing criteria and a testing schedule for the incident management plan. The process should address scope, types of tests, what to test, scenario creation, objectives, and testing frequency.

Criteria For “Yes” Response:

  • The organization conducts incident response tabletop exercises that include ransomware response scenarios at least annually.

questions.title: UM:I.Q05
questions.text: Is least privilege enforced through technical (technology based) restrictions?
questions.supplemental:
Question Intent: To determine if the principle of least privilege is enforced through technical means to control user access.

Least privilege is the restriction of privileges to only those accounts that require them to perform their duties, while limiting accounts to only those privileges that are truly necessary. Doing this reduces the exposure of those privileges to a smaller, more easily manageable set of accounts. Local administrative accounts and accounts for software program management and installation are particularly powerful, but have small scopes of control and should be restricted as much as possible.

Grant access and admin permissions based on the principles of need-to-know and least privilege. Restrict user access to only the information, networks, hardware, and applications necessary.

Questions to consider:
  • Are you asking why someone, or something, needs privileged access?
  • Does the marketing team need access to the company’s financial transactions?
  • Does the reservations team need access to social media sites?
  • Does a junior analyst need management-level admin/ configuration privileges?
Answering these questions helps you identify and implement need-to-know and least privilege to lower the risks of malware infections, data breaches, and insider threats.

Technical implementations of least privilege can include:
  • Assigning users to specific groups with certain privileges applied
  • Assigning user working hours
  • Using machine-based restrictions
  • Employing separate processing domains for finer grain allocation of user privileges
  • Restricting privileged accounts to specific personnel or roles
  • Using location-based restrictions
Criteria for “Yes” Response:
  • The organization uses technological means to enforce the principle of least privilege for all users.

questions.title: UM:I.Q06
questions.text: Are audit logs maintained for all privileged (e.g. system administrator) accounts?
questions.supplemental:
Question Intent: To determine if audit logs are maintained for all privileged accounts.

An audit log is a record of the events occurring within an organization’s systems and networks. Logs are composed of log entries; each entry contains information related to a specific event that has occurred within a system or network. Many logs within an organization contain records related to computer security. These computer security logs are generated by many sources, including security software, such as antivirus software, firewalls, and intrusion detection and prevention systems; operating systems on servers, workstations, and networking equipment; and applications.

Possible actions:
  • To determine the set of auditable events, organizations should consider the auditing appropriate for each of the security controls to be implemented.
  • To ensure that the current set of auditable events is still appropriate, a periodic review should be performed.
  • Information system audit records should be periodically (as defined by the organization) reviewed for indications of inappropriate or unusual activity.
  • Audit information and audit tools should be protected from unauthorized access, modification, and deletion.
  • Organizations should retain audit records until it is determined that they are no longer needed for administrative, legal, audit, or other purposes.
Criteria for “Yes” Response:

questions.text: Is a physical incident response exercise performed at least once a year?
questions.supplemental:
Question intent: To determine if the organization performs physical incident response exercises at least once a year.

Incident response testing should progress in stages, such as:

  • plan review
  • tabletop test or walkthrough
  • component testing, such as incident declaration and team notification
  • limited scenario testing, using an isolated incident or a single-category incident as in an IT failure
  • large-scale incident testing, using a regional disaster or pandemic and testing cross-plan dependencies

By testing your incident response plan, you allow your organization and the personnel directly involved in managing incidents the opportunity to practice roles and responsibilities in a controlled environment. You also ensure that the plan produces the desired outcomes when tested. Incident management exercises are not meant to result in pass/fail “grades.” Instead, they should be viewed as opportunities to measure plan performance and to expose any unexpected outcomes, conflicts, and needed improvements in a controlled environment.

Possible Actions:

  • Guidelines and standards for incident management plan exercises can include the following:
    • Identification and responsibilities of plan owners
    • Identification and involvement of stakeholders
    • Exercise management
    • Plan exercise schedule
    • Requirements for what information must be documented during and after a plan exercise
    • Measures for how the organization evaluates incident management plan performance

  • Exercise plans
    • Test plans developed using pre-established exercise criteria

  • Plan exercise results
    • Define acceptable response times and process adherence in accordance with the plan

  • Strategy for testing and maintaining the incident management
    • Establish guidelines for plan testing; using lessons learned to improve the incident management plan
Criteria for “Yes” Response:
  • The organization performs a physical incident response exercise at least once a year.

IT staff should be trained so that they can maintain their networks, systems, and applications in accordance with the organization’s security standards.

Comprehensive role-based training addresses management, operational, and technical roles and responsibilities covering physical, personnel, and technical safeguards and countermeasures.

Question Intent: To determine if security hardening guides are used to manage system configurations.

  • include instructions or procedures for configuring an IT product to an operational environment

  • Documentation (e.g., text file) that guides the checklist user to manually configure an IT product
  • Documents that explain the recommended methods to securely install and configure a device
  • Policy and programmatic documents that set forth guidelines for such things as auditing, authentication mechanisms (e.g., passwords), and perimeter security

questions.title: UM:I.Q08
questions.text: Is rogue hardware being detected?
questions.supplemental:
Question Intent: To determine it rogue hardware is being detected by the organization

Learn what is on your network. Establish and maintain an accurate, detailed, and up-to-date inventory of all organizational assets. Ensure the inventory records the asset description, network address (if static), hardware address, machine name, enterprise asset owner and custodian, etc. for each asset, and whether the asset has been approved to connect to the network. Review and update the inventory of all enterprise assets on a periodic basis. Inventorying authorized hardware and knowing the physical location and user of that hardware allows for unauthorized hardware to be identified and removed.

Possible actions:
  • Develop a process to determine if unauthorized or rogue hardware exist on the network and to address rogue hardware assets on a periodic basis. The enterprise may choose to remove the asset from the network, deny the asset from connecting remotely to the network, quarantine the asset, etc.
  • Ensure a policy addressing the addition of unauthorized hardware to the organization’s networks is developed. The policy should, at a minimum, indicate that adding unauthorized hardware to the organization’s networks is prohibited.
  • The policy should also direct that awareness training be developed to train users of the issues surrounding the addition of unauthorized or rogue hardware to the organizations networks.
Criteria for “Yes” Response:
  • The organization is periodically detecting rogue hardware that is connected to its networks.

questions.title: IR:I.Q08
questions.text: Has the organization implemented redundant systems where appropriate for the purpose of resiliency?
questions.supplemental:
Question Intent: To determine if the organization has implemented redundant systems where appropriate for the purpose of resiliency.
  • Availability. The system’s availability (i.e., reliability) requirements are an important factor in design. Systems with strong availability/up-time requirements may require more redundancy.
  • Maintaining functionality during adverse conditions. This involves designing the industrial control systems (ICS) so that each critical component has a redundant counterpart. Additionally, if a component fails, it should fail in a manner that does not generate unnecessary traffic on the ICS or other networks, or does not cause another problem elsewhere, such as a cascading event. The ICS should also allow for graceful degradation such as moving from "normal operation" with full automation to "emergency operation" with operators more involved and less automation to "manual operation" with no automation.
The organization must plan to sustain technology assets to ensure the continued operation of services. Mechanisms implemented to achieve this practice can take many forms:

  • load balancing: a method that improves the distribution of workloads across multiple resources to optimize resource use, maximize throughput, minimize response time, and avoid overload of any single resource
  • hot swap capabilities: the ability to replace or add components without stopping or shutting down the associated system
  • high availability implementations: a failover methodology to ensure availability during device or component interruptions
  • alternate telecommunications services
  • alternate processing sites
  • fail-safe procedures:
    • fail-safe: a design feature or practice that, in the event of a specific type of failure, inherently responds in a way that will cause no or minimal harm to system assets, property, or life
    • Fail-safe procedures may include alerting operator personnel and providing specific instructions on subsequent steps to take (e.g., do nothing, reestablish system settings, shut down processes, restart the system, or contact designated organizational personnel).
Criteria for “Yes” Response:
  • The organization has implemented redundant systems where appropriate for the purpose of resiliency.

questions.title: UM:A.Q09
questions.text: Are users who attempt to install rogue hardware counseled against installing rogue hardware?
questions.supplemental:
Question intent: to determine if users who attempt to install or connect rogue or unauthorized hardware to the organization’s networks are counseled against adding rogue devices to the organization’s networks.

Ensure a policy addressing the addition of unauthorized hardware to the organization’s networks is developed. The policy should, at a minimum, indicate that adding unauthorized hardware to the organization’s networks is prohibited.

The policy should also direct that awareness training be developed to train users of the issues surrounding the addition of unauthorized or rogue hardware to the organizations networks.

Possible actions:
  • Develop or update security policies to ensure rogue or unauthorized hardware is addressed.
  • Develop a process to determine if unauthorized or rogue hardware exist on the network and to address rogue hardware assets on a periodic basis.
  • Develop or update awareness training to address the topic of rogue hardware.
  • Conduct awareness training.
  • Evaluate the effectiveness of the awareness training with respect to connecting rogue hardware to the network, and revise as needed.

Criteria for “Yes” Response:
  • The organization counsels all users who attempt to install rogue or unauthorized hardware to the organization’s networks.
